entity.name: Richard Wagner
entity.description: The composer who built his own opera house to stage his vision. German creator of epic music dramas including the 15-hour Ring cycle, Wagner revolutionized opera with leitmotifs and the concept of the Gesamtkunstwerk. His antisemitic writings remain deeply controversial. He fled Germany as a revolutionary fugitive, was rescued from poverty by a Bavarian king, and died in Venice.

story.name: Richard Wagner
story.description: Flees Dresden as a revolutionary, spends 12 years in exile, persuades a king to fund his vision, and builds a custom opera house in Bayreuth for a 15-hour cycle. The most ambitious ego in music history.

moments.name: Richard Wagner Is Born in Leipzig's Jewish Quarter
moments.subtitle: The future antisemitic polemicist enters the world in a neighborhood of Jewish merchants
moments.description: On May 22, 1813, Richard Wagner was born at No. 3, the Brühl — known as the House of the Red and White Lions — in Leipzig's Jewish quarter. He was the ninth and youngest child of Carl Friedrich Wagner, a police clerk, and Johanna Rosine Wagner. His father died of typhoid fever six months after Richard's birth. His mother then lived with the actor Ludwig Geyer, whom Wagner believed for years to be his biological father. The irony that Germany's most notorious antisemitic composer was born in a Jewish neighborhood has not escaped historians.

moments.name: Wagner Flees Dresden After Joining a Failed Revolution Against the King
moments.subtitle: An opera composer becomes a wanted fugitive alongside the anarchist Mikhail Bakunin
moments.description: In May 1849, the May Uprising erupted in Dresden against King Frederick Augustus II of Saxony. Richard Wagner, then Royal Saxon Court Conductor, played a supporting role in the revolution alongside the Russian anarchist Mikhail Bakunin. When the uprising was crushed, warrants were issued for the revolutionaries' arrest. Wagner fled first to Paris, then to Zurich, beginning 12 years of exile from Germany. During this period he could not attend performances of his own operas. The exile proved creatively fertile: Wagner conceived the entire Ring cycle and wrote the revolutionary essays that outlined his theory of the Gesamtkunstwerk.

moments.name: Wagner Premieres Tristan und Isolde, the Opera That Changed Music Forever
moments.subtitle: Its opening chord is so ambiguous that theorists still debate what key it is in
moments.description: On June 10, 1865, Richard Wagner's Tristan und Isolde premiered at the National Theatre in Munich under conductor Hans von Bülow, funded by Wagner's patron King Ludwig II of Bavaria. The opera's radical harmonic language — particularly its famous opening "Tristan chord" — pushed tonal music to its breaking point, using extreme chromaticism and endlessly deferred resolution. Music scholars regard Tristan as a pivotal precursor to modernism. The premiere was a sensation, though overshadowed by scandal: Wagner was having an affair with Cosima von Bülow, the conductor's wife, who would later become Wagner's second wife.

moments.name: Wagner Opens His Custom-Built Opera House with the Complete Ring Cycle
moments.subtitle: A 15-hour, four-opera saga performed in a theater designed for one composer's works alone
moments.description: On August 13, 1876, the Bayreuth Festspielhaus opened with the first complete performance of Richard Wagner's Der Ring des Nibelungen — a cycle of four operas totaling roughly 15 hours. Wagner had spent years fundraising and overseeing construction of the theater, which featured innovations like a hidden orchestra pit and a fan-shaped auditorium designed to blend instrumental sound before it reached the audience. Kaiser Wilhelm I, Emperor Pedro II of Brazil, and King Ludwig II attended. The Festspielhaus remains devoted exclusively to Wagner's works and hosts the annual Bayreuth Festival, still managed by Wagner's descendants.

moments.name: Wagner Dies of a Heart Attack in a Venetian Palace
moments.subtitle: His wife Cosima lies beside the body for 25 hours, refusing to leave
moments.description: On February 13, 1883, Richard Wagner suffered a fatal heart attack at the Palazzo Vendramin Calergi in Venice, where he had been wintering with his family. He was 69 years old. His wife Cosima was so distraught that she lay beside his body for 25 hours and reportedly cut off her hair to place in the coffin. Wagner's body was transported by gondola and then by train back to Bayreuth, where he was buried in the garden of his villa, Wahnfried. The Palazzo Vendramin Calergi later became Venice's municipal casino, and today a plaque and small museum mark the room where Wagner died.
